### **Building a Security Culture That Runs Without You:** A Case Study on Democratizing Application Security and Autonomous Lifecycle Integration


*Written By:*[Naveen Rajamannar](https://www.linkedin.com/in/naveen-rajamannar/?lipi=urn%3Ali%3Apage%3Ad_flagship3_profile_view_base%3BwAtpKdbCTXuktntUkz4VZQ%3D%3D)


At DV, application security spans hundreds of developers and thousands of repositories. Product teams ship data products, UI and API service platforms, agentic workflows, plugins and chatbots weekly, with only a few AppSec team members to support the workload. Security knowledge travels by word of mouth, with each team having to repeat the findings.


While mature DevSecOps principles and robust automation tools could cover this, what if security engineers stopped being the only people who do security testing and instead became the ones who build the systems that empower everyone else?


Over the past year, that is exactly what our team has designed and built. This guide details how we democratized application security, transferring true ownership across engineering by embedding automated security checks directly into pre-existing developer and QA workflows, and learned from each other to make security a shared, cross-functional mindset.


### The Challenge


The biggest bottleneck in security was never tools; it was access and confidence. Developers and QA engineers already ran thousands of test cycles. What they needed was a security vocabulary and tooling they could use in their workflows without a security engineer in the room. Below is a representation of the main building blocks of security democratization.


### Establishing a Common Language and Training: OWASP


DevSecOps is exceptionally easy to put on a slide deck, but difficult to execute in reality. The first thing we did was not write a pipeline or configure a new scanner; instead, we established a common technical vocabulary that every engineer could reference and plan a security championship program around. The OWASP standards provided that open framework. We anchored our platform on a comprehensive matrix of industry standards, mapping our baseline to OWASP ASVS, backend pipelines to the API Top 10, UI scenarios to the WSTG, and AI-specific risks to the LLM Top 10.


But raw compliance standards alone do not change day-to-day engineering behavior. Partnering with L&D, we launched a Confluence program that stripped away complex jargon to focus on short, practical engineering examples. By leveraging video-generation tools DV makes available to us, like Google Vids and Gemini Canvas, we built an asynchronous library of bite-sized videos and high-impact instructional material engineers could easily absorb between meetings.


#### Transferring Capability: Prompt Files


Knowledge that lives in a separate place, even when well-designed, only gets referenced when people remember to reference it. This insight came from observing how QA teams worked: they started adopting prompt files, structured instructions and reusable templates used directly in the IDE.


Security testing workflow: quick question-based code generation


Security should be built into where the work is already happening, not in a different place as a separate task. Instead of asking QA engineers to consult a knowledge base before writing tests, we built security directly into the prompt files they were already using, which were also designed to use the same tools that QA already uses: Postman scripts, Newman execution and Playwright code with pre-built security assertions. **No new tool required mastery, because security was never meant for learning something new and complex.**


#### From Prompt Files to IDE commands: The MCP Step


Prompt files lowered the barrier. But they still required a developer to find the file, set it up, and choose how to run it. Through Model Context Protocol (MCP), the security testing capability was embedded directly into the IDE as a native command. A developer working in Cursor, Copilot, or Claude already had the security skills loaded. Running a full OWASP API security scan meant typing one command.


Test output in the IDE: each OWASP category surfaces a Watch Video link alongside the evidence and scenario count


Prompt files transferred the knowledge. MCP embedded the capability into the places where people already worked. Each layer made security more automatic and accessible, with humans in the loop and in the right places.


Taking this further, we built an interactive MCP-based system with **PromptFlow MCP** (in-house MCP, not Microsoft Azure PromptFlow) that has custom skills, resources and tools to be built and plugged in. We engineered the security-specific skills and tools on top of this framework. Answering a few questions activates the right flow for the requirement at hand, handling everything from simple username-and-password logins to complex auth flows. This scaled our intended design across all projects without requiring manual execution in each one. Since it takes contextual input from the tester, each team’s product knowledge also gets directly ingrained into the security process.


Because engineers never had to leave their existing workflows, security never felt like a separate step. This question-driven, context-aware model also became the basis for what was coming next: autonomous agents that could carry that same intelligence and operate end-to-end within the Quality Engineering agentic workflow.


### Automation: Security Scripts Inside the QA Workflow


Automation is powerful, but it’s most effective when it is woven directly into the daily habits of individual contributors. The defining power of our decentralized framework is that security scans are no longer separate, isolated events scheduled by an outside AppSec team on a disparate cadence. Instead, they run natively inside the exact same GitLab CI/CD pipelines as functional QA suites, triggered automatically by the exact same merge request events. A developer merges code, the functional test suite runs, and security runs right alongside it.


This pipeline alignment was entirely deliberate. Because the underlying tests are structured in formats that QA and development teams already understand, there was no new complex tooling to learn. The output looks and feels exactly like any standard unit or integration run. To prevent engineering fatigue, we rolled out OWASP coverage in systematic phases. This gave product delivery teams ample time to ingest initial findings, ask architectural questions, and build natural habits before the next set of test categories and automated assertions arrived.


### The Final Milestone of Our Vision: Autonomous AI Agents


The next milestone we have been building toward is the rollout of fully **Autonomous AI Agents** . Operating within a highly extensible AI framework engineered by our QA Automation Center of Excellence (CoE) team, we deployed our first two autonomous security agents: api-security-gen and web-security-gen (with many more currently in the pipeline).


These agents independently discover live application endpoints, generate relevant test code, map assertions to explicit OWASP categories, build extensive test scenarios, execute them dynamically, and deliver comprehensive, triage-ready reports.


But the more interesting question is not who can call the agents, but what else can call them? For example, the **orchestrator agent** integrates with our project management lifecycle, where code modifications automatically trigger the orchestrator to generate targeted performance suites in the background. Security suites can be triggered the same way if configured similarly.


Second, the orchestrator agent leverages a crawler network that runs on demand as new crawl requests come in, mapping live application changes and feeding fresh feature surfaces into our test pipelines with minimal manual configuration.


### Dashboards Live Where the Audience Lives


While standard analytics monitoring platforms like Grafana worked beautifully for our initial baseline metrics, we intentionally routed this program’s telemetry straight into the environments our teams live in every day: Confluence and GitLab. Given the complex cross-team collaboration required for this rollout, utilizing rich HTML allowed us to break free from standard dashboard constraints, giving us the design freedom and future flexibility we needed to serve different audiences.


We engineered a dedicated background pipeline that systematically parses the artifacts created during every QA pipeline run. It aggregates this data into two distinct visibility layers tailored for separate audiences:


1. **The Management Confluence View:** A high-level pane tracking roadmaps, adoption rates, and portfolio volumes so leadership instantly understands their security posture without sync meetings.


2. **The Engineering GitLab Pages View:** A granular, squad-level dashboard mapping per-project timelines, code sources, endpoint coverage, and explicit execution results over time.


### The Heavy Lifting Behind the Seamless Automation


Flawless automation is the visible outcome that stakeholders see, but **relentless manual groundwork is the engineering grit** that knits separate tools together and enables the entire process to move forward as one cohesive unit, making an advanced AI ecosystem look effortless.


To bridge the gap between cold automation pipelines and fluid engineering workflows, we focused our deepest engineering energy on an intensive, human-centric rollout playbook:


- **Culture and Enablement:** Shared OWASP vocabulary, video libraries, Security Champions Program, embedded initial security QA engineer with QA teams, and security built directly into existing QA frameworks with no new tools.
- **Workflow Integration:** Security prompts in existing QA workflows, MCP as native IDE commands in Cursor, Claude and Copilot, functional QA suites and Security suites side-by-side.
- **Framework Architecture:** PromptFlow MCP, autonomous api-security-gen and web-security-gen agents, passive crawler network for live endpoint discovery, and automated data pipelines publishing to Confluence and GitLab Pages.
- **Closing the Loop:** Embedded feedback loops feeding every human-identified gap back into the next automation cycle.


The first instinct was to provide the tools to the team and step back. Alas, it did not work; access is not the same as ownership. Handing a developer a security scanner without the vocabulary to read what it returns, or having the expectation that fixing it is their job, just produces unread reports.


As a result, we slowed down. We recruited a dedicated security QA engineer to sit directly with the QA teams and do the groundwork by hand first: running the early tests with them, translating findings into language that made sense in their context, and learning where people actually got stuck. That manual phase is what made the self-serve model possible later. You cannot hand off ownership of something you have not first walked through together.


The manual groundwork paid off.


### The Payoff: Measurable Real-World Impact


By treating security as an integrated, shared engineering responsibility rather than a separate compliance checkbox, the platform has achieved verifiable scale across its portfolio:


- **76.47% Overall Adoption:** Across 17 active API portfolio projects, 13 have completely adopted automated security testing, achieving 100% endpoint coverage.
- **20,454 Security Tests Executed per Cycle:** Over twenty thousand distinct security assertions are run autonomously every cycle across active delivery pipelines, maintaining a remarkably stable **success rate** .


Historically, executing a comprehensive DevSecOps transformation required massive, specialized security teams and immense effort. By leveraging native tools that engineering squads already possessed, using context-aware autonomous AI agents, and prioritizing meticulous human scaffolding, this entire **orchestration groundwork** platform was successfully planned, built, and shipped on roughly a **20% to 30% time allocation** alongside standard daily AppSec workloads.


Let’s see how it stacks up against the DevSecOps Principles:


The security backlog is no longer AppSec’s exclusive queue to manage. It belongs directly to the people who write and test the code, a self-learning asset completely adapted to the way our engineering teams actually work.
